extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for choosing, formatting, and replacing dialogue tags in fiction; covers which tags to use, when to use action beats instead, punctuation rules, common mistakes, and lists of tag verbs by function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a dialogue tag
rubrics_metrics.description: A dialogue tag (also called a speech tag or attribution) connects a line of dialogue to the character who speaks it; it typically contains a subject and a speaking verb (e.g., "she said").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tag tells the reader who spoke without drawing attention to itself; used well, dialogue tags are invisible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutral dialogue tags should predominate
rubrics_metrics.description: Neutral tags disappear on the page — the reader processes them without noticing. Use these most often.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed: said, asked, replied, answered, added, continued, noted, mentioned, stated, responded. "Remember: the neutral tags should make up the vast majority of your attributions. The others are seasoning, not the main course."

rubrics_metrics.name: Use volume tags sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Tags that show volume indicate how loudly or quietly a character speaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed: whispered, murmured, muttered, mumbled, shouted, yelled, screamed, bellowed, called, hollered, hissed, breathed. Use sparingly to indicate volume when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use emotion tags selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Tags that convey how a character feels while speaking can show emotion, but overuse weakens their impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed: cried, sobbed, wailed, moaned, groaned, sighed, laughed, giggled, chuckled, snickered, sneered, snarled, growled, snapped, barked. Reserve for moments where the dialogue alone doesn't show emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use manner-of-speech tags to show style/quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Tags that describe the quality or style of speech can clarify how something is said.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed: stammered, stuttered, babbled, rambled, drawled, slurred, croaked, rasped, wheezed, lisped, chirped, sang, cooed, purred. Use to convey particular speech patterns sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intent tags to reveal purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Tags that show the speaker's intent reveal why the character is speaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed: demanded, insisted, urged, pleaded, begged, warned, cautioned, threatened, promised, suggested, proposed, offered, confessed, admitted, declared, announced, proclaimed. Use when the purpose behind the words matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use uncertainty/thought tags for thinking aloud
rubrics_metrics.description: Tags that show uncertainty or inner thought are appropriate when a character is thinking aloud or unsure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed: wondered, mused, pondered, reflected, considered, speculated, guessed, supposed, ventured, theorized. These signal internal questioning or speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer action beats when you want to show rather than tell
rubrics_metrics.description: An action beat replaces the dialogue tag with a physical action that identifies the speaker and adds characterization, emotion, or pacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example contrast: Dialogue tag: "We need to leave now," she said urgently. Action beat: "We need to leave now." She shoved clothes into a bag without folding them. "The action beat is stronger because it shows urgency through behavior rather than telling the reader with an adverb." Use action beats to reveal character, build tension, or ground dialogue; use tags when the conversation itself is the focus and you don't want to slow it down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comma before the tag when tag follows the quote
rubrics_metrics.description: When the dialogue tag follows the quote, use a comma inside the closing quotation mark, not a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct example: "I'll be there," she said. Incorrect: "I'll be there." She said. This is a common punctuation error to watch for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lowercase the tag after the quote
rubrics_metrics.description: The dialogue tag is part of the same sentence as the dialogue, so it starts with a lowercase letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct example: "I'll be there," she said. Incorrect example (capitalized): "I'll be there," She said.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a period and capitalize when an action follows (not a speech verb)
rubrics_metrics.description: If what follows the dialogue is an action (not a speech verb), use a period and capitalize the action sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct: "I'll be there." She grabbed her coat. Incorrect: "I'll be there," she grabbed her coat. Treat actions that identify the speaker as separate sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep question marks and exclamation points (don’t add comma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Question marks and exclamation points stay in place and replace the comma; do not add a comma after them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct: "Are you coming?" she asked. Incorrect: "Are you coming?," she asked.

rubrics_metrics.name: When the tag comes before the quote, follow with a comma
rubrics_metrics.description: If the tag precedes the quoted material, put a comma after the tag before the opening quotation mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: She said, "I'll be there." Also shown: She said "I'll be there." (the guide shows the comma rule — include a comma after the tag).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using too many fancy tags ("said is dead" pitfall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing 'said' with colorful verbs everywhere makes tags the story and pulls attention from dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide notes that said and asked account for the overwhelming majority of dialogue tags in published fiction, and that overusing verbs like 'exclaimed' or 'proclaimed' draws attention. Keep 'said' and 'asked' as your default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't use impossible speaking verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: If the verb doesn't describe a way of producing sound, it's an action, not a dialogue tag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and explanation: You can't 'smile' a sentence or 'shrug' words. "Nice weather," he shrugged — that's an action, not speech. Treat such words as action beats (period after dialogue, capitalize the action).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-relying on adverbs in tags
rubrics_metrics.description: An adverb in the tag (e.g., 'she said angrily') often indicates weak dialogue or missed opportunities for showing emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the dialogue doesn't convey the emotion, an adverb won't fix it. Strong dialogue and well-chosen action beats eliminate most '-ly' adverbs. When tempted to use adverbs, ask whether dialogue or surrounding action can carry the emotion instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't tag every line in a two-person conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: In a two-person exchange, readers can follow alternating lines once the rhythm is established; you don't need an attribution on every line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drop in a tag or action beat every three to four lines to keep readers oriented, but let the conversation breathe in between.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice regularly to improve dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Great dialogue comes from consistent practice and habit-building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide recommends daily practice (e.g., using a distraction-free editor and daily streak tracking) to sharpen dialogue-writing skills, implying that frequency and deliberate practice are part of craft improvement.
